chapters.title: Chapter 1: What History Means by a Cycle

lessons.title: Why Markets Move in Cycles, Not Straight Lines

body.text: Over decades, markets have climbed. Over months and years, they have swung hard in both directions. If you expect a straight line, the swings will scare you out at the worst possible moment.

children.text: In April 1979 the Sensex stood at 100. In September 2024 it touched roughly 86,000. That works out to about 16% a year before dividends, over 45 years. It sounds like a smooth ride. It was not. Along the way the index lost more than half its value three separate times. This course is about those swings: why they happen, how they have played out across three centuries of market history, and what they mean for anyone investing today.
The Straight Line Your Brain Wants to Draw

Humans are wired to extrapolate. If the Nifty has gone up for three years, the easy assumption is that it will keep going up. If it has fallen for six months, the easy assumption is that it will keep falling. Both assumptions feel like common sense, and history shows that both are regularly wrong at exactly the moments they feel most certain. A cycle is simply the pattern that makes straight-line thinking fail: periods of rising prices and optimism, followed by periods of falling prices and pessimism, repeating with no fixed length or size.

body.title: Two ways to look at the same market

columns.label: Straight-line thinking
points: A three-year rally proves the market is safe
A 30% fall means something is permanently broken
Buys most after long rallies, sells most after long falls

columns.label: Cycle-aware thinking
points: Recent returns say little about the next few years
A long rally usually means prices and expectations are stretched
Deep falls have happened repeatedly and have been recovered from, for broad Indian indices so far
Keeps investing on a plan rather than on a mood
Expects turns, without pretending to know their timing

body.text: Both statements are true at the same time: the Sensex compounded at roughly 16% a year for 45 years, and anyone holding it lived through several falls of more than 50%. The long-run return was the reward for sitting through the cycle, not a return earned by avoiding it.

children.text: Trend Plus Cycle: Two Forces in Every Price

markDefs.definition: Price to earnings ratio: the share price divided by earnings per share. It tells you how many rupees investors are paying for every rupee of annual profit.

children.text: A useful way to see where cycles come from is to split a share price into two parts. The first is earnings per share, what the business actually makes. Over long periods, Indian corporate earnings have grown with the economy and with inflation, and that growth is the upward trend. The second is the
P/E ratio
, the multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings. The multiple is driven by mood, interest rates and expectations, and it swings far more than earnings do. That swing is the cycle.

body.caption: Earnings drive the long-term trend. The multiple drives most of the cycle.
Same business, same earnings growth, three different outcomes. EPS grows 12% a year for 5 years, from ₹50 to ₹88.1. Starting price: ₹50 × 25 = ₹1,250

children.text: The business did exactly the same job in all three rows. The investor's result ranged from almost nothing to nearly 20% a year, purely because of where the multiple sat in its cycle. This is not just theory. Hindustan Unilever is a well-known recent case: its profits grew between 2021 and 2024, yet its share price in 2024 was only modestly above its late 2021 level, because the market steadily paid a lower P/E for it. You can check the earnings and P/E history yourself on screener.in.

body.title: Calculate the Cycle Effect
body.prompt: A stock has EPS of ₹40 and trades at a P/E of 20. Over the next four years EPS rises to ₹60 and the P/E expands to 30. What is the total percentage gain in the share price?
body.explanation: Starting price = ₹40 × 20 = ₹800. Ending price = ₹60 × 30 = ₹1,800. Gain = (1,800 − 800) ÷ 800 = 125%. Earnings grew only 50%. The other part of the gain came from the multiple expanding, which is the cycle working in your favour. Run it in reverse and the same multiple can take that gain away.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Nifty 50 earnings grow 15% in a year, but the index ends the year exactly where it started. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The index data is wrong, because prices must follow earnings every year
The P/E multiple fell by about 13%, cancelling out the earnings growth
Companies cut dividends, which reduces the index level
Earnings have no connection to index levels
body.explanation: Price = EPS × P/E. If EPS rises by a factor of 1.15 and price is unchanged, the P/E must have fallen by a factor of 1 ÷ 1.15, about 0.87, which is a 13% drop in the multiple. Over a single year the multiple can easily overpower earnings. Over decades, earnings usually win.

children.text: Why Cycles Keep Happening

If everyone knows markets move in cycles, why don't the cycles disappear? Because the forces behind them are built into how economies and people work. Four matter most, and later lessons cover each in depth:
Human emotion:
rising prices pull in new buyers, which pushes prices higher still. Falling prices trigger selling, which pushes prices lower still. Greed and fear reinforce themselves in both directions.
Credit:

in good times banks lend freely and people borrow to invest, including through margin trading. When lending tightens, that borrowed money has to be repaid and assets get sold. Lesson 1.3 covers this engine.
The business cycle:
companies expand capacity when demand is strong, often all at once, then face overcapacity and falling margins. Profits rise and fall with it.
Policy:

the RBI raises interest rates to cool inflation and cuts them to revive growth. Governments spend more in slowdowns and less in booms. Every one of these responses changes what investors are willing to pay for earnings.

body.text: A cycle is not a clock. No Indian bull or bear market has followed a fixed schedule. The COVID fall of 2020 lasted about two months, while the Sensex took nearly three years after its January 2008 peak just to close above that level again. Anyone selling you a precise cycle timing system is selling you false confidence.

children.text: Why the Down Leg Hurts More Than It Looks

Falls and recoveries are not symmetrical. If your ₹1,00,000 portfolio drops 50% to ₹50,000, a 50% gain only takes it back to ₹75,000. You need a 100% gain to get back to where you started. The deeper the fall, the steeper the climb, and the longer the calendar time it can take.

body.label: Time to recover: two very different cycles
body.context: The Sensex closed above its January 2008 high only in November 2010. The Nifty regained its January 2020 high by November 2020. Same kind of event, completely different recovery time.

content.caption: Fall and gain both written as decimals, so a 40% fall is 0.40
Gain needed to get back to the previous peak

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: If the Nifty falls 20% from its peak, it needs to rise ___% from the bottom to get back to that peak.
body.explanation: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.20) − 1 = 1 ÷ 0.80 − 1 = 0.25, or 25%. A 20% fall followed by a 20% rise still leaves you 4% below the peak.

cards.definition: The repeating pattern of rising and falling prices, driven by emotion, credit, business conditions and policy. Cycles repeat, but with no fixed length or size.
The long-run direction of prices, mostly set by growth in earnings over many years.
The highest point of a cycle, before prices turn down.
The lowest point of a cycle, before prices turn up.
The percentage fall from a peak to the trough that follows it.
A rise (re-rating) or fall (de-rating) in the P/E multiple investors pay, independent of any change in earnings.

body.title: The Colleague Who Draws Straight Lines
body.scenario: It is September 2024. The Nifty is above 26,000 and has roughly doubled from its March 2020 low. A colleague at your office in Pune says: "The market only goes up now. I'm taking a ₹5 lakh personal loan at 14% to put into small-cap stocks on Zerodha. Four years of data can't be wrong."
body.prompt: Using what you learned in this lesson, what is wrong with your colleague's reasoning, and what specific risks does the loan add?
body.modelAnswer: Your colleague is drawing a straight line through the up leg of a cycle. Four strong years say very little about the next four: in Indian market history, long rallies have repeatedly been followed by sharp falls, including drawdowns of more than 50% in 1992, 2000 and 2008. Strong rallies also tend to push P/E multiples up, which means part of the recent gain came from the multiple, and multiples can contract even if earnings keep growing. The loan makes it much worse. The 14% interest has to be paid every month whatever the market does, so the investment has to beat 14% a year just to break even. If small caps fall 30%, a 43% rise is needed just to recover, while EMIs keep running, and your colleague may be forced to sell at the bottom to meet them. In fact the Nifty fell more than 15% from that September 2024 peak over the following months, and small caps fell considerably more. The cycle-aware approach is to invest surplus money, not borrowed money, and to expect falls rather than be shocked by them.

children.text: Cycles are not new, and they are not an Indian quirk. Economists have been trying to measure and name them for over a century, and some of their ideas still shape how professionals think about markets. The next lesson looks at the four classic cycle theories and what they get right and wrong.

body.text: Index levels in this lesson are approximate and rounded, and are used for education only. Past market behaviour does not guarantee future results. Nothing here is investment advice. For advice on your own situation, consult a SEBI registered investment adviser.

points: Markets move in cycles, not straight lines: the Sensex grew from 100 in 1979 to about 86,000 in 2024, yet fell more than 50% three times on the way
Share price = EPS × P/E. Earnings growth drives the long-term trend, while swings in the P/E multiple drive most of the cycle
The same business can deliver about 1% or about 20% a year depending only on how the multiple moves
Cycles persist because of human emotion, credit, the business cycle and policy responses, and none of these go away
Cycles have no fixed length: the Sensex took nearly three years to regain its 2008 peak, while the Nifty regained its 2020 peak in about ten months
Falls and recoveries are asymmetric: a 50% fall needs a 100% gain to recover
Extrapolating recent returns, especially with borrowed money, is the classic way investors get hurt by cycles
